newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE -- Colombian truckers' strike wreaks havoc.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE -- Colombian truckers' strike wreaks havoc.

text.p: A strike by Colombian truck drivers has wreaked havoc on the economy and underscored the ease with which key industries like coffee can be paralyzed at the drop of a hat.

The strike by the Colombian Truck Drivers Association (ACC), a federation representing about 90,000 drivers nationwide, was played down by the government after it began at midnight on October 13. But private coffee exporters said it succeeded almost immediately in halting all shipments to the nation's ports, and the world's No. 2 coffee producer was basically put straight out of business as soon as it began. "We're totally paralyzed," Victoria Barriga, a commercial representative at Expocafe Ltda, a Bogota coffee exporter, said Wednesday. "You can't move any coffee." Another exporter, who asked not to be named, said the strike had already forced delays in the shipment of about 350,000 60- kilo bags of coffee promised for delivery in October. And he predicted that "real panic" would erupt in world markets by early November if the strike continued into next month.
"There's going to be a rush for every single bean that is uncommitted," he said.

Colombia's aging railway network is in a notorious state of disrepair, a fact that goes a long way toward explaining the effectiveness of the strike since less than one percent of the country's inland cargo moves by train. The government hopes to change this beginning next month, when it is tentatively set to start auctioning off rail concessions to the private sector.

That offers no solution to the current strike, however, and the government unveiled a series of measures Wednesday aimed at ending the 10-day-old stoppage by force if necessary. The measures were announced by Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, acting head of state during President Ernesto Samper's visit to Asia.

They included a call on the police and military to move immediately to clear any and all barricades erected across highways by strikers over the past week. The government also ordered provincial governors and mayors to take any steps deemed necessary to reestablish transportation in their jurisdictions and said authorities had been instructed to arrest anyone fostering a breakdown in law and order or the disruption of normal transport services. Additionally, Serpa said the office of Prosecutor-General Alfonso Valdivieso had been instructed to launch a official investigation into possible "economic crimes" stemming from the work stoppage, which was declared illegal by the government on October 18. Serpa also reiterated earlier threats that truckers backing the strike would have their operators' licenses revoked if they failed to return to work. The ACC, which called the strike to press for higher pay for drivers and lower taxes and tolls, defiantly vowed to continue the work stoppage despite the government's threat of possible mass arrests. -- Bogota newsroom, (571) 610 7544 REUTER
